paragraphs.source_en: The day after my master dreamed of boasting about his watercolor painting, the aesthete with the gold-rimmed spectacles, who had not shown his face for many days, came to visit him. No sooner had he seated himself than he opened with, “How is the painting coming along?” My master replied with perfect composure, “Following your advice, I have been applying myself to sketching from life. Indeed, by sketching from life one seems able to understand fully the forms and subtle changes of color one had never noticed before. It appears that because the West advocated sketching from life long ago, painting has achieved what it has today. Andrea del Sarto was worthy of his fame.” He did not breathe a word about the diary, but once again expressed his admiration for Andrea del Sarto. The aesthete laughed, scratched his head, and said, “To tell the truth, my dear fellow, I made that up.” “Made up? Made up what?” My master still did not realize that he had been made a fool of. “What do you mean, what! Why, that Andrea del Sarto you keep admiring so fervently. That was something I invented on the spot. I never imagined you would believe it so earnestly. Ha, ha...” The aesthete was vastly pleased with himself. Listening to this conversation from the veranda, I could not help wondering in advance how my master would record the matter in today’s diary. This aesthete was a man whose sole pleasure lay in scattering baseless nonsense about and hoaxing people with it. He seemed not to have given the slightest thought to what resonance the Andrea del Sarto affair had set vibrating in my master’s emotional strings, and triumphantly went on chattering, “No, really! When I make a joke now and then, people take it seriously; a joke can provoke a tremendous comic aesthetic sensation, and that is amusing indeed! Not long ago I told a student that Nicholas Nickleby had advised Gibbon not to write his life’s great work, The History of the French Revolution, in French, and so he published it in English instead. That student turned out to have an extraordinary memory, and at a lecture meeting of the Society of Japanese Literature he solemnly repeated my words exactly; it was extremely funny. And at the time there were about a hundred people in the audience, all listening with the utmost attention! There is another amusing story: the other day, at a gathering where some literary men were present, when someone brought up Harrison’s historical novel Theophano, I immediately remarked, ‘That is the finest of historical novels; the scene depicting the heroine’s death in particular is so gloomy and terrifying that it sends a ghostly chill through one.’ As soon as I said this, a Mr. Know-it-all sitting opposite me chimed in, ‘Quite so, quite so, the description of that passage is truly superb.’ From that I knew the fellow, like me, had not read the novel either.” My master, who suffers from nervous dyspepsia, opened his eyes wide and asked, “If you talk such nonsense and the other person has actually read the book, what on earth would you do?” My master’s words sounded as if deceiving people were no problem, and the only awkward thing was being exposed and left with no way out.

paragraphs.source_zh: 主人梦中自诩水彩画的第二天，那位多日未露面、脸上架着金丝眼镜的美学家来拜访主人了。他刚一落座，就开口问道：“画得怎样啦？”主人不动声色地回答说：“按你的忠告，我正在努力写生。的确，通过写生，似乎能充分了解过去不曾注意的形体、色彩的微妙变化等。看来，西洋很早就主张写生，所以绘画才有今天这样的成绩。真不愧是安德里亚·特尔·萨尔德哩。”日记的事，他只字未提，却对安德里亚·特尔·萨尔德又钦佩了一番。美学家一边笑，一边搔着头说：“实说吧，老兄，那是我瞎编造的。”“编造？编造什么？”主人受到愚弄还不知道。“你还问呢！就是你一味钦佩的那个安德里亚·特尔·萨尔德呗。那是我随意编造的。真没料到你竟会如此地信以为真。哈哈……”美学家十分得意。我在廊前听了这番对话，禁不住先琢磨起来：“不知主人在今天的日记上怎样记下此事。”这位美学家喜欢胡诌一些无影无踪的事儿来愚弄人，还专门以此为乐。他似乎根本没考虑安德里亚·特尔·萨尔德这件事会在主人的情弦上拨弄出什么样的音响，便又得意洋洋地接着说道：“哪里！我经常开个玩笑，人们就把它当真，玩笑可以挑起很大的滑稽美感，真有意思！不久以前，我告诉一个学生说，尼古拉斯·尼克尔贝曾经劝告基朋，不要用法文撰写其毕生大作《法国革命史》，结果他改用英文出版了这部作品。谁知那个学生记忆力特别强，在一次日本文学会的讲演会上，他就一本正经地把我的话重复了一遍，真是滑稽得很。而当时听讲的有一百人左右，竟然也个个在那里洗耳恭听哩！还有一件有趣的事儿：前些天在一次有文学家参加的聚会上，有人提出哈里森的历史小说《塞奥伐诺》的时候，我当即评论说：‘那是历史小说中的白眉，尤其刻画女主人公之死的那一段，写得真是阴森可怕，鬼气袭人。’我这么一说，坐在对面的一位万事通先生马上接着说：‘不错，不错，那段情节的描写真是妙极啦。’我由此知道那家伙也和我一样，并没有读过这部小说。”患神经性胃病的主人听后，睁大了眼睛问道：“你这样胡说八道，如果对方读过那部书，岂不糟糕啦？”主人的话使人感到仿佛骗人是没关系的，只是露了马脚下不了台。

paragraphs.source_en: At this the aesthete, entirely unmoved, said, “No matter. In that case one need only say one has confused it with another book.” Having said this, he laughed, “heh, heh.” Though this aesthete wore gold-rimmed spectacles, in character he really did resemble Blacky from the rickshawman’s house. My master smoked a Sunrise cigarette, blowing smoke rings, with an expression that seemed to say, “I have no such courage.” The aesthete’s eyes also seemed to say, “It is precisely because you lack such courage that your paintings will never amount to anything.” The aesthete then continued, “Still, jokes are jokes, but painting really is a terribly difficult thing. It is said that Leonardo da Vinci once had his pupils draw the stains on a church wall. Indeed, if you observe carefully the damp, leaking wall when you go to the privy, you will find there an exceedingly fine design formed entirely by nature. Try paying close attention and sketching it; you are sure to produce an interesting picture.” “You are deceiving me again, aren’t you?” “Not at all. This time it is true. What a penetrating remark it is! Only da Vinci could have said such a thing.” My master said, “Yes, it certainly is penetrating.” My master was half convinced; however, even to this day he seems not to have gone sketching in the privy.
